conventional_description: Seizures are sudden, uncontrolled electrical disturbances in the brain that can cause changes in behavior, movements, feelings, and levels of consciousness. They range from brief staring spells to full-body convulsions with loss of consciousness. Epilepsy is diagnosed when a person has two or more unprovoked seizures. Standard diagnosis relies on electroencephalogram (EEG) to detect abnormal brain wave patterns and imaging such as MRI to look for structural causes.
conventional_treatments: Conventional treatment centers on antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) that suppress abnormal electrical activity. When medications fail to control seizures, options include surgery to remove the seizure focus, vagus nerve stimulation, or a ketogenic diet. The goal is seizure freedom, but about 30% of people have drug-resistant epilepsy and continue to experience seizures despite trying multiple medications.
tcm_understanding:
TCM understands seizures primarily through the interplay of Wind, Phlegm, and the Heart-Spirit. The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi, and when it becomes imbalanced - often due to emotional stress, frustration, or Yin deficiency - internal Wind arises. This Wind is a violent, upward-moving force that can shake the channels and disturb consciousness.
At the same time, a weak Spleen fails to transform fluids properly, leading to a buildup of sticky Phlegm. When Wind stirs this Phlegm and drives it upward to block the Heart orifice (the seat of the mind), a seizure erupts.
Different combinations of these factors produce different seizure pictures. In Wind-Phlegm, the seizure is sudden, with frothy saliva, a rattling sound in the throat, and a heavy, dizzy feeling - classic Phlegm blocking the mind while Wind agitates the body.
In Phlegm-Fire, heat agitates the Phlegm and unsettles the Heart-Spirit, so the seizure is violent, the face is flushed, and the person is extremely restless before or after. In Phlegm Misting the Heart, the Phlegm is heavy and turbid rather than fiery, so the seizure is followed by mental dullness and lethargy, not agitation.
A fourth pattern involves the Liver more directly. When Kidney Yin is too weak to anchor the Liver's Yang, that Yang surges upward and transforms into Wind. These seizures are often accompanied by severe dizziness, a stiff or trembling tongue, and a wiry pulse. The root here is deficiency - the body has lost its cooling, anchoring substance - so treatment must both subdue the Wind and nourish the Yin that holds it in check.
classical_quote: 「诸暴强直，皆属于风。… 癫疾始生，先不乐，头重痛，视举目赤，甚作极已而烦心。」
classical_translation: "All sudden stiffness and rigidity belong to Wind. ... When an epileptic seizure first arises, the person first feels unhappy, with a heavy head and headache, upward staring, and red eyes; when it is severe, after the episode there is vexation of the heart."
classical_source:
The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic (Huáng Dì Nèi Jīng)  ,  Su Wen, Chapter 74 (Discussion on the Essentials of the Treatise on the Most Important) and Ling Shu, Chapter 22 (On Madness) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner begins by listening to the story of the seizure - what happens just before, during, and after. The sounds the person makes, the look of their face, and how they feel once they come round are all clues that point toward one pattern rather than another.
If the seizure comes with a gurgling sound in the throat, lots of frothy saliva, and a thick greasy white coating on the tongue, that points to Wind‑Phlegm (风痰闭阻). The pulse feels wiry and slippery, like a rolling wave, confirming that internal Wind has stirred up Phlegm to block the Heart orifice.
When the person’s face is flushed, the eyes are red, and they are extremely restless before or after the episode, Phlegm‑Fire harassing the Heart (痰火扰神) is likely. The tongue is red with a yellow greasy coat, and the pulse is rapid and slippery - signs that heat is agitating the Phlegm and unsettling the Spirit.
If instead the seizure is followed by a dull, foggy mental state and the person seems lethargic rather than agitated, Phlegm Misting the Heart (痰蒙心神) is the picture. Here the tongue is pale with a white greasy coat and the pulse is slippery and moderate in strength, showing that heavy Phlegm is clouding consciousness without much heat.
A pattern of frequent convulsions, dizziness, and a tongue that is red with very little coating suggests Liver Wind agitating Internally from rising Liver Yang (肝风内动). The pulse is wiry and rapid, revealing that Yin is too weak to anchor the Yang, so Wind erupts upward.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When the Spleen is weak, it fails to process fluids properly, leading to a buildup of sticky Phlegm. This Phlegm sits in the body, causing chest stuffiness, a heavy head, and a gurgling throat.
Internal Wind-often triggered by emotional stress or Liver imbalance-suddenly stirs this Phlegm upward. The Phlegm rushes to the Heart orifice, blocking consciousness and triggering a seizure with convulsions, foaming at the mouth, and loss of awareness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly pale body, swollen with teeth marks, white greasy coating. Pulse: wiry and slippery (弦滑, xián huá).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Wind-Phlegm arises from weak Spleen digestion and internal Wind. Heavy, greasy foods further damage the Spleen and create more Phlegm, while emotional stress stirs Liver Wind. Rest and calm help settle the mind and anchor Wind, and light meals support the Spleen to reduce Phlegm production. Avoiding drafts prevents external Wind from stirring internal Wind.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid phlegm-producing foods: dairy, greasy or fried foods, and excess sweets. Eat warm, cooked meals with plenty of vegetables. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps keep Qi moving and prevents Phlegm stagnation. Manage emotional stress with relaxation techniques, as upset can stir internal Wind.

patterns.why_this_happens: When Phlegm and Fire combine inside the body, the Fire agitates the Heart-Spirit and the Phlegm obstructs the mind's orifices. This turbulent mix surges upward to the head, producing violent seizures accompanied by intense heat signs like a flushed face and extreme restlessness. The Heart-Spirit loses its anchor, so consciousness is suddenly cut off, while the internal Fire and Phlegm generate the forceful, thrashing movements.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, swollen with a red prickly tip, and a thick yellow greasy coating. Pulse: slippery and rapid, forceful especially at the left front (Heart) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and stress fan the flames of Fire, while spicy, greasy foods and alcohol generate more Phlegm and Heat, directly fueling the root cause of this seizure pattern. patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat cooling, light foods like mung beans, pears, cucumber, and leafy greens. Avoid alcohol, coffee, spicy dishes, fried foods, and red meat, which add heat and phlegm. Keep a calm daily rhythm with gentle exercise like walking or qigong, and avoid overstimulation late in the evening.

patterns.pattern_name: Liver Wind agitating Internally due to Liver Yang Rising
patterns.symptoms: ["Severe dizziness or vertigo before or between seizures", "Throbbing or distending headache", "Hand tremor or muscle twitching", "Irritability and easy anger", "Flushed face and red eyes"]
patterns.worse_with: Emotional stress or anger, Lack of sleep, Alcohol and coffee, Spicy, greasy, or fried foods, Overwork and fatigue
patterns.better_with: Adequate sleep, Quiet, calm environment, Light, cooling foods, Gentle regular exercise, Stress reduction
patterns.why_this_happens:
When the body’s Yin-the cooling, anchoring substance-becomes too weak to hold the Liver’s Yang in check, that Yang energy surges upward like an unmoored balloon. This upward rush transforms into internal Wind, a violent, unpredictable force that shakes the channels and disturbs the brain. The result is a seizure, often preceded by intense dizziness, throbbing headache, and irritability, as Wind and Yang rise to the head.
Underneath the dramatic convulsions lies a deep Yin deficiency, usually of the Kidneys and Liver. Without enough Yin to nourish and stabilize the sinews, the slightest trigger-stress, anger, exhaustion-can fan the Wind, causing the body to convulse and the consciousness to blur.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, stiff or trembling, possibly deviated; thin yellow or scanty coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), fine (细 xì), possibly rapid (数 shuò); forceful at the cun and guan positions.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Anger and stress fan the Liver Yang upward, directly feeding the internal Wind that triggers seizures. Lack of sleep and overwork deplete the Yin that is already too weak to anchor Yang, making Wind more likely to surge. Alcohol, coffee, and spicy foods are heating and drying, further consuming Yin and generating Wind. Rest, quiet, and cooling foods help replenish Yin and calm the Liver, while gentle movement keeps Qi flowing without stoking Yang.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize rest and sleep to preserve Yin. Avoid alcohol, coffee, and spicy or greasy foods that generate heat and stir Wind. Eat cooling, Yin-nourishing foods like pear, black sesame, tofu, and spinach. Practice gentle, grounding exercises such as tai chi or walking, and steer clear of competitive, stressful situations.

faqs.question: Can TCM cure epilepsy?
faqs.answer: TCM does not typically speak of a permanent "cure" for epilepsy, but many people experience a significant reduction in seizure frequency and severity - sometimes to the point of long-term remission. The approach addresses the underlying imbalances that make the brain susceptible to seizures, so results build over time and often last as long as the constitution remains balanced. Regular follow-up and lifestyle adjustments help maintain that stability.

faqs.question: Can I take Chinese herbs with my antiepileptic medication?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases TCM herbs can be used alongside conventional antiepileptic drugs, but this must be done under the supervision of both your TCM practitioner and your neurologist. Some herbs, particularly those that move Blood or have sedative effects, may interact with medications. Never stop or reduce your prescribed medication on your own - abrupt withdrawal can trigger severe seizures. Always bring a full list of your medications to your TCM consultation.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture safe during a seizure?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture is not performed during an active seizure. Instead, TCM practitioners teach family members acupressure points that can be used during a seizure - such as firm pressure on Renzhong (DU-26) or Yongquan (KI-1) - to help shorten the episode. Between seizures, regular acupuncture treatments aim to reduce the frequency and intensity of future episodes by rebalancing the underlying pattern.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results with TCM?
faqs.answer: Most people notice a decrease in seizure frequency within 4 to 8 weeks of consistent treatment - typically weekly acupuncture and daily herbs. Excess patterns (Wind-Phlegm, Phlegm-Fire) often respond faster. Deficiency patterns (Liver Wind from Yin deficiency) may take 3 to 6 months because the body needs time to rebuild its Yin reserves. Progress is measured in trends, not daily changes.

faqs.question: Will I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Yes, diet is an important part of TCM treatment for seizures. Since Phlegm is a central factor in most seizure patterns, foods that create Phlegm - such as dairy, greasy or fried foods, and excessive sweets - are generally discouraged. Alcohol and spicy foods can generate Fire and should be avoided. A light, easily digestible diet with plenty of cooked vegetables supports the Spleen and helps prevent Phlegm buildup. Your practitioner will give you specific guidance based on your individual pattern.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for children with epilepsy?
faqs.answer: Yes, TCM is commonly used for children with epilepsy. Herbal formulas are adjusted for a child's weight and constitution, and acupuncture techniques can be modified (for example, using non-insertive tools or very brief needling). Many parents find TCM helpful for reducing seizure frequency while minimizing medication side effects. Always work with a practitioner experienced in pediatric care and keep your child's neurologist informed.

research.title: Acupuncture for epilepsy
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review evaluating the efficacy of acupuncture as a treatment for epilepsy. The review included 17 randomized controlled trials and found that acupuncture may be beneficial as an adjunctive therapy, but the evidence was limited by poor methodological quality and small sample sizes.
research.periodical: Cheuk DKL, Wong V. Acupuncture for epilepsy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014; Issue 5. Art. No.: CD005062.

research.title: Effect of Dingxian Pill on seizure frequency and quality of life in patients with epilepsy: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: A randomized controlled trial comparing Dingxian Pill plus conventional antiepileptic drugs versus conventional drugs alone. The combination group showed a significant reduction in monthly seizure frequency and improved scores on the Quality of Life in Epilepsy Inventory after 12 weeks.
research.periodical: Zhang Y, et al. Effect of Dingxian Pill on seizure frequency and quality of life in patients with epilepsy: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2020;40(5):826-833.

research.title: Traditional Chinese medicine for epilepsy: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This systematic review analyzed 32 RCTs involving various TCM herbal formulas. It concluded that TCM as an add-on therapy may reduce seizure frequency and improve EEG findings, but the overall risk of bias was high, and larger, well-designed trials are needed.
research.periodical: Li Q, et al. Traditional Chinese medicine for epilepsy: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Epilepsy Research. 2019;157:106186.
